newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH TRADE GAP JUMPS, ANALYSTS SEE POSITIVE TREND.
newsitem.headline: CZECH TRADE GAP JUMPS, ANALYSTS SEE POSITIVE TREND.

text.p: The Czech trade deficit for the first two months of 1997 nearly doubled, year-on-year, but analysts said that despite the jump, the data were in-line with expectations and show a favourable trend for sagging exports.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) on Monday said the February trade gap was 13.7 billion crowns, pushing the January-February shortfall to 27.2 billion crowns, up from 16.2 billion over the first two months of 1995.
A Reuters forecast of economists had predicted a 14.5 billion crown deficit for February.

"It is clear that the figures for the first two months are in accordance with the majority of forecasts for a deficit for the whole year of under or around 200 billion crowns," said Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka.
Added Vladimir Kreidl, an economist at Patria Finance: "The figures are slightly better than expected."
The CSU has forecast a trade deficit of 211-219 billion crowns for 1997 after a record 160.3 billion crown gap in 1996.
The bureau said in a statement that imports over the two months totalled 123.1 billion crowns, a 9.1 percent year-on-year increase, while exports contracted 0.7 percent to 95.9 billion crowns.
Janacek noted that despite a contraction in exports, year-on-year, the figure is an improvement over January when exports contracted by some 2.5 percent.
"There is a slight improvement for exports. I think that we can expect a recovery in exports from the second quarter of the year," he said.
The CSU added that imports of raw materials and machinery remain at the heart of the deficit, accounting for some 81 percent of the goods brought into the country.

Analysts said that this figure could be expected as industry undergoes major restructuring, though it remains to be seen if the imports are being used efficiently and will translate into economic growth.
"There is no space for saying that everything is okay (because of the January-February results)...This single figure doesn't change anything, its only slightly better than expected," said Kreidl.

The trade figures come in the wake of better than expected GDP figures. On Friday, the CSU said fourth quarter 1996 GDP rose 4.7 percent reversing a steady downtrend from the first quarter which had prompted calls for an interest rate cut to stimulate the economy.

The Czech crown strengthened slightly on the trade data, rising some 40-50 basis points to around 1.4 percent above its dollar/mark basket parity. The central bank fixed the crown on Monday at +1.32 percent, up from +0.88 percent on Friday.
"The trade figures are in line with what we expected. (But) the CNB (central bank) will definitely not cut interest rates," said Petr Tomek, a forex dealer at Zivnostenska Banka.
The CNB last increased its key interest rate, the discount rate, last summer as part of a series of tightening moves to choke a burgeoning money supply and ease inflation.
The discount rate was raised one full percentage point to 10.5 percent. At the same time, the CNB hiked repo rates and raised minimum reserve requirements to 11.5 percent from 8.5 percent.

The moves appear to be working, with the M2 money supply, which measures currency, demand deposits, time and savings deposits, and foreign currency deposits, easing to 7.8 percent in December from 20.2 percent in the same month of 1995.
In addition, inflation has continued its gradual easing, dipping to 7.3 percent year-on-year in February.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
